source.title: Identifying and reporting position-specific countermovement jump outcome and phase characteristics within rugby league

paper.citation: McMahon J., Lake J., Comfort P. Identifying and reporting position-specific countermovement jump outcome and phase characteristics within rugby league. PLOS ONE. 2022;17:e0265999. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0265999.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Which countermovement-jump force-time and outcome variables differ between rugby-league forwards and backs, and how should individual results be presented alongside position norms? Participants: Fifty-four senior men's English Rugby League Championship players: 27 forwards and 27 backs. Sport and level: Senior professional-level rugby league. Design: Cross-sectional observational comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three countermovement jumps on a force platform.
paper.tldr: No countermovement or propulsion phase variable differed significantly by position; effects were small or less, with P values at least 0.09 and effect sizes no larger than 0.46. Backs jumped higher and had greater take-off velocity, with P = 0.03 and an effect size of 0.60. Select CMJ variables from the decision they are intended to support.
paper.methods: Design: Cross-sectional observational comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three countermovement jumps on a force platform. Comparator: Global forwards versus backs. Measurements and outcomes: Countermovement and propulsion phase variables, jump height, take-off velocity, take-off momentum, and body mass. Analysis: Between-position significance tests, effect sizes, and individual-data visualization.
paper.findings: No countermovement or propulsion phase variable differed significantly by position; effects were small or less, with P values at least 0.09 and effect sizes no larger than 0.46. Backs jumped higher and had greater take-off velocity, with P = 0.03 and an effect size of 0.60. Forwards produced greater take-off momentum, with P < 0.01 and an effect size of 1.01, but individual outcomes overlapped considerably between positions.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional study cannot show how the selected variables respond to training, fatigue, injury, or changes within an athlete. Global forward/back categories may conceal meaningful role and body-size differences; the observed individual overlap limits deterministic position classification.
paper.practicalImplications: Select CMJ variables from the decision they are intended to support. Jump height and momentum describe different performance expressions, and body mass strongly shapes their positional meaning. Use position distributions as context, then prioritize within-athlete longitudinal change and uncertainty rather than labeling a player from the position mean alone.
